body: A cold-water Chondrus crispus gel with additions. The listing names baobab, elderberry and hibiscus, and the words in front of them are various ingredients like.

That phrase is the problem. It names three things and leaves the rest open, so there is no complete declared list to print here. The base is the same plant that carries Northern Soul and is sold on its own as the plain gel.
One to two tablespoons a day, morning or early afternoon, as the listing has it.

Straight off the spoon, or mixed into juice, a smoothie, or a tea with raw honey. If you miss a day, do not take double the next one. Seaweed carries iodine and there is an upper limit on how much of that you want in a day.

ingredients.intro: The listing names a base and three additions, and the phrase it uses in front of them is various ingredients like. That phrase is why this section has four cards and the sheet below has a blank where the declared list should be.

cards.alt: Flat forking red seaweed, wet, on shingle
cards.p: The base. Picked by hand off cold Atlantic rocks at low tide, flat forking fronds that dry dark. This is the plant the old herbals call carrageen, and it is the same base that carries Northern Soul and is sold on its own as the plain gel.

The listing says baobab and names no species. There are several trees in the genus and the fruit of more than one is traded, so this card stops at the genus. The fruit is a hard pod with a dry pale pulp inside, and it is that pulp which is powdered.

cards.alt: A cluster of black elderberries on the bush
cards.p: The listing says elderberry and gives no Latin name. In this country the word means Sambucus nigra, the black elder of hedgerows and roadsides. The berries are cooked or dried before use and are not eaten raw.

The listing says hibiscus and names no species. The hibiscus used as a food is the deep red calyx of Hibiscus sabdariffa, dried, which is what makes the sharp red infusion people know. Our label does not confirm that is the one, so this card stops at the genus.

spec.smallprint: Contains iodine from seaweed. Do not exceed two tablespoons a day. Speak to your GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement, particularly if you have a thyroid condition, low blood pressure, or take medication for either. Food supplements should not be used as a substitute for a varied and balanced diet and a healthy lifestyle. Keep out of reach of young children.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The base is named in Latin, the two sizes and two prices are printed, the serving is printed, and the caution the listing carries is printed word for word. The list of what else is in the jar is not complete, and that sits on the sheet as a blank rather than a guess. What a spoonful does in the body is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: Why this page has the most blanks on the site
paras: Every page here has a row or two I cannot fill in. This one has more of them than any other, and I would rather you saw them together than found them one at a time.

The reason is a phrase on the listing. It says various ingredients like baobab, elderberry and hibiscus. Like is not a list. It names three things and leaves the door open behind them, and while that door is open I cannot print a complete declared list, a vegan mark, or anything at all about proportions.

What I can tell you is the base, which is the same cold-water Chondrus crispus that goes into Northern Soul and into the plain jar. The two sizes and the two prices. The serving, and the times of day the listing gives for it. The caution about blood pressure, which is on the listing and which I have printed here as it stands rather than softening it.

If you want a sea moss jar where every line on the sheet is filled in today, that is Northern Soul. Come back to this page when the label has caught up, because the rows above are the ones that will change.
